title: Mean daily flow concentration exceeded historical estimates across 69 Victorian gauges in 2010-2019
abstract: We tested the share of annual flow in the highest 5% of observed daily flows at Victorian gauges. We used CAMELS-AUS v2.03 and fitted separate historical models with annual flow volume, daily rain concentration and seasonal rain fractions. Coverage rules retained 69 gauges, 2,608 training rows in 1950-1996 and 662 test rows in 2010-2019. The mean observed-minus-predicted share across gauges was +5.64 percentage points. Its conditional 95% spatial and time block interval was +1.86 to +10.32 points. A check with 1,000 training refits gave limits of +1.47 to +11.47 points; some resampled fits lost rank. The observed post-period share was 36.37%; the model predicted 30.73%. This is a model residual, not a raw increase of 5.64 points. Complete years, SILO rain, a bounded response model and individual training-range restrictions retained positive intervals. A historical test gave uncertain squared-error improvement from the rain terms and a negative mean residual. The result limits this fixed conditional relation. It does not identify a drought cause, groundwater loss, larger absolute floods or a permanent change. Selected and nested gauges, short time support, measurement error and model form limit inference. The package gives code, aggregate evidence, resampling draws, a static figure, source hashes and repeat instructions. External source records and derived gauge databases stay outside the signed bundle.

display.caption: Daily flow concentration at 69 Victorian gauges. The left panel shows annual observed and modelled means; gauge coverage can change by year. The grey band marks 1997-2009. The middle panel gives equal-gauge 2010-2019 mean residuals and 95% intervals. The right panel gives sensitivity checks. Positive residuals mean greater annual flow concentration than the fixed historical relation predicts. These are conditional model results, not estimates of a causal drought effect.
